Abstract
Modern container ships face higher wind loads due to increased windage areas, making acurate predictions of wind loads esential
for moring design. Existing empirical models, largely developed for container ships with smaler windage areas and simpler
geometrical congurations than those of modern large-scale vesels, often lack acuracy and do not acount for the inuence of
nearby structures. This study proposes a multi-delity surogate modeling framework for the prediction of wind-load coecients,
combining empirical corelations with simplied and detailed CFD models for ships in open-sea and harbor environments. The
aproach relies on recursive co-kriging to consistently fuse information acros delity levels, enabling acurate predictions at a
reduced computational cost. A sensitivity analysis is used to identify the most inuential geometric parameters, and the resulting
reduced parameter space is explored through sequential sampling to eciently construct the training database.
The surogate models are validated over a wide range of loading congurations and for two distinct harbor environments. The
results demonstrate that the multi-delity aproach signicantly improves prediction acuracy compared to single-delity models,
while substantialy reducing the reliance on high-delity simulations. In particular, the proposed framework captures the depen-
dence of wind loads on key geometric parameters and consistently outperforms traditional empirical corelations, providing a robust
and ecient tol for enginering aplications.
Keywords: container ships, wind loads, multi-delity surogate modeling, Gausian Proces regresion, Computational Fluid
Dynamics, harbour environments
1. Introduction
Container ships acount for aproximately 90% of global
merchandise trade. In recent decades, vesel size has increased
dramaticaly [1, 2, 3], with some ships exceding 20,0 TEU,
acompanied by a signicant growth in windage area. As a re-
sult, modern vesels are increasingly susceptible to wind loads
and extreme weather conditions. This isue is particularly crit-
ical in harbour environments, where ships are manoeuvred in
conned spaces and are frequently subjected to moring opera-
tions. Complex port layouts can induce chaneling and shelter-
ing eects, leading to increased uncertainty in wind force coef-
cients. Such uncertainties may have severe consequences, in-
cluding los of control during manoeuvres or failure of moring
lines, potentialy resulting in high-risk acidents and signicant
economic loses. Several incidents reported in [4] highlight
the role of unexpected wind loads during storms in colision
events and unmoring operations. These chalenges have mo-
tivated the development of automated moring systems within
so-caled smart ports [5], which require acurate and real-time
prediction of wind loads.
Wind loads are traditionaly obtained from wind tunel ex-
periments performed on scaled ship models, for which exten-

sive databases are available in the literature [6, 7, 8]. Based on
these data, empirical corelations have ben developed over the
past decades [9, 10, 1] to estimate wind loads for dierent ship
geometries, loading congurations, and angles of atack. How-
ever, these corelations are typicaly derived from simplied
representations of ship superstructures and are not fuly rep-
resentative of modern large-scale container vesels. Moreover,
they generaly neglect the inuence of the surounding harbour
environment, which can signicantly alter the eective wind
loads.
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) provides an alterna-
tive aproach to predict wind loads at ful scale by resolv-
ing the ow around detailed ship geometries and their envi-
ronment. A substantial body of literature adreses Reynolds-
averaged NavierStokes (RANS) simulations of ships in open
sea [12, 13, 14], with dierent container arangements [15],
in harbour congurations [16, 4], and in side-by-side scenar-
ios [17]. Several studies [16, 14] have also investigated the
impact of geometrical simplications on predicted wind loads.
While simplied geometries may introduce distortions in the
aerodynamic response [14], they signicantly reduce computa-
tional cost and enable broader exploration of loading congura-
tions and operating conditions. Nevertheles, high-delity CFD
simulations remain computationaly demanding, often requir-


ing hours to days on standard workstations, which limits their
aplicability in real-time or large-scale parametric analyses.
To overcome these limitations, surogate models can be
employed to emulate wind load predictions based on avail-
able data. Recent studies have explored machine learning ap-
proaches, including Articial Neural Networks (ANs) [18, 19,
20, 21] and Gausian Proces regresion [2]. These models
are capable of handling complex, high-dimensional relation-
ships betwen input parameters and wind load coecients. For
instance, [18] developed AN-based models using container
stack information and wind angle as inputs for multiple vesel
types. Alternative parametrizations of loading congurations
have ben proposed using Fourier-based descriptors [20, 2],
enabling more compact representations of ship geometry. Other
works [19] have employed convolutional neural networks to
predict presure elds, combined with dimensionality reduction
techniques such as Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and au-
toencoders.
Despite these advances, existing surogate modeling ap-
proaches remain limited by the availability of high-delity data.
Generating acurate CFD datasets is computationaly expen-
sive, restricting the coverage of the design space and the gen-
eralization capabilities of the resulting models. On the other
hand, simplied models and empirical corelations, while les
acurate, provide inexpensive but informative aproximations
of the underlying physics. This sugests that combining infor-
mation from multiple delity levels could provide an eective
strategy to balance acuracy and computational cost.
In this work, a multi-delity surogate modeling framework
is proposed for the prediction of wind loads on container ships.
The aproach combines empirical corelations, simplied CFD
simulations, and high-delity CFD models within a unied
Gausian Proces regresion framework [23].
By exploiting
the corelation betwen data sources of dierent delity, the
method enables acurate predictions while signicantly reduc-
ing the number of expensive high-delity simulations required.
A sensitivity analysis is used to identify the most inuential
geometric parameters, and a sequential sampling strategy is
employed to eciently explore the reduced parameter space.
The predictive capability of the proposed aproach is asesed
acros a wide range of loading congurations and extended to
dierent harbour environments.
The remainder of the paper is organized as folows.
The
mathematical formulation of the multi-delity surogate model
for wind loads and its feature selection are described in sec-
tion 2. Section 3 describes the data-sources of various delities
employed to train the surogate, while section 4 explains the
training algorithm. The results of the training are provided in
section 5. Conclusions and outloks are given in the last section
6.

3. Data-sources
In this work, the surogate models are trained using data from
multiple sources of increasing delity. These data sources dif-
fer in terms of physical modeling complexity and computa-
tional cost, and are combined within the recursive multi-delity
framework introduced in Eq. (13).
The lowest-delity (LF) data are provided by empirical cor-
relations (Section 3.1), while computational uid dynamics
(CFD) simulations are used to generate higher-delity data. A
simplied CFD model is employed as a medium-delity (MF)
source (Section 3.3), whereas a detailed CFD model provides
high-delity (HF) data (Section 3.2).
The denition of the delity hierarchy depends on the tar-
get aplication. For surogate models predicting wind loads
in open-sea conditions, the detailed CFD model represents the
highest-delity level. For surogate models targeting specic
harbour environments, the hierarchy is extended by introducing
an aditional level: the detailed CFD model in open-sea con-
ditions is treated as an intermediate delity, while the highest-
delity data are provided by detailed CFD simulations includ-
ing harbour structures.
The validity of this hierarchical structure is asesed a pos-
teriori through the consistency of the multi-delity model. The
dierent data sources and their coresponding delity levels are
described in the folowing subsections.

Abstract: Modern container ships face higher wind loads due to increased windage areas, making acurate predictions of wind loads esential for moring design. Existing empirical models, largely developed for container ships with smaler windage areas and simpler geometrical congurations than those of modern large-scale vesels, often lack acuracy and do not acount for the inuence of nearby structures. This study proposes a multi-delity surogate modeling framework for the prediction of wind-load coecients, combining empirical corelations with simplied and detailed CFD models for ships in open-sea and harbor environments. The aproach relies on recursive co-kriging to consistently fuse information acros delity levels, enabling acurate predictions at a reduced computational cost. A sensitivity analysis is used to identify the most inuential geometric parameters, and the resulting reduced parameter space is explored through sequential sampling to eciently construct the training database. The surogate models are validated over a wide range of loading congurations and for two distinct harbor environments. The results demonstrate that the multi-delity aproach signicantly improves prediction acuracy compared to single-delity models, while substantialy reducing the reliance on high-delity simulations. In particular, the proposed framework captures the depen- dence of wind loads on key geometric parameters and consistently outperforms traditional empirical corelations, providing a robust and ecient tol for enginering aplications.
